News.title: My mum was brutally stabbed to death in front of me when I was just 2 – she took a heartbreaking secret to her grave
News.content:
RACHEL Nickell would be 57 now if it weren’t for the fateful events of July 1992.

The 23-year-old was stabbed 49 times and sexually assaulted on a sunny weekday morning on Wimbledon Common, while she walked with her two-year-old son.





A horrified passer-by later found Alex clinging to his slain mother’s blood-soaked body crying “wake up mummy”.

The now 36-year-old has revealed that his mum might have been pregnant at the time of her death.

Rachel and her partner André Hanscombe had decided to have an abortion eight months prior, a decision Alex says Rachel never recovered from and his father still regrets.

Speaking to the Daily Mail he says: “It was very early on and I’ll never truly know. But I know she never would have wanted us to make the same mistake again.”



The dad and son have given the lost little girl the name Inés and light a candle for her and Rachel when they go to mass.

The pair have now given their first major newspaper interview together ahead of a new Netflix drama about Rachel’s murder being released this week.

André waved goodbye to Alex and Rachel that Thursday morning as he left their flat in Balham, southwest London.

He says: “I will never forget the two of them smiling warmly at me, standing on the steps, hand in hand. Alex joyfully and playfully, and Rachel as lovingly as always.”

The former model then took Alex for a walk in the park when she was killed by serial sex offender Robert Napper.



He lurched from bushes and attacked her in a frenzied knife attack.

Rachel’s throat was slit, with cuts on her hands showing she had put up a fight.

Tragically, little Alex had stuck a piece of paper on Rachel like a plaster “to make mummy better”.



A huge police investigation was launched and 14 men were arrested in connection with her murder but all of them were released.

As the probe turned out more dead ends, officers put pressure on Alex to provide the smoking gun that could catch his mum’s killer, as he had a near perfect recollection of the attacker.

This demand on the traumatised toddler caused dad André to move them both to the South of France and later Barcelona.

The police investigation continued in the UK after the father and son moved abroad and on September 21, 1992, cops targeted Colin Stagg.

The 29-year-old newspaper delivery man had been fined £200 after he pleaded guilty to indecent exposure on Wimbledon Common.



No forensic evidence linked Stagg to the scene but cops asked criminal psychologist Paul Britton to create an offender profile of the killer and decided he was their prime suspect.

Just months later, the trial collapsed after the judge condemned a police undercover operation in which a female officer exchanged a series of letters with Stagg.

The prosecution withdrew its case and Stagg was formally acquitted in September 1994 and later given more than £700,000 in compensation.



It was not until 2008, 16 years after the attack, that Robert Napper, then 41, admitted stabbing Rachel.

Napper had been a patient at Broadmoor Hospital for more than ten years suffering from paranoid schizophrenia and Asperger’s.

He had been convicted of killing Samantha Bisset and her four-year-old daughter Jazmine in November 1993 – 16 months after Rachel was slain.



Advances in DNA profiling meant police were able to link Napper to the murder in 2004.

He was convicted of her manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility.

A CPS dossier leaked to André and Alex reveals a host of police failings and missed opportunities, including Napper’s own mother contacting the police to say her son had confessed to raping a woman.

The records reveal he may have assaulted and raped as many as 90 women, this claim has not been disputed by the police.

André says Napper is a victim himself in many ways and he and Alex have forgiven him.

He adds: “Abused as a child, abandoned by his family, failed by the system. The wounds we carry can make us capable of terrible evil.”

The Witness will be available to stream on June 4, along with a three-part drama series based on the murder.

News.title: Dark side of honeymoon hotspot with 112 tourists killed in ‘deathtrap’ dives, drownings & horror boat propeller deaths
News.content:
MARVELLING at a stunning coral reef through crystal-clear waters, Brit tourist Elaine Richmond had no idea her holiday was about to turn fatal.

The experienced diver was swept away by a powerful current and killed on the paradise island she had visited for decades, with her devastated husband Malcolm dying days later. Her death is one of a number of tragedies in the honeymoon destination. And now, experts have revealed why so many have suffered the same fate.



With its white-sand beaches, turquoise lagoons and breathtaking scenery, the Maldives has long been a favourite escape for loved-up couples and keen divers – and its popularity is only gaining.

Some 160,000 Brits jetted off to the tropical paradise last year, marking a 16 per cent increase from the year before.

But as visitor numbers soar, a number of deaths and injuries in its pristine waters have tarnished the archipelago’s romantic image.



The dangers were laid bare in recent weeks after five Italian tourists died while diving in a cave near the Vaavu Atoll.

At least 112 tourists died in marine-related incidents in the Maldives from 2020 to 2023 – including 42 deaths linked to diving and snorkelling, official statistics show.

Meanwhile, 8 British tourists have drowned in the hotspot since 2021, according to the UK Foreign Office.

Experts warned that powerful currents are just one of the hidden dangers lurking beneath the Maldives’ picture-perfect waters, as well as sharks and even boat propellers.

Dr Keiron Fraser, who runs one of the largest scientific diving programmes in Europe, told The Sun: “In and out of the atolls between islands and in those channels, the current is pretty strong.



“That’s probably one of the things that I would say is quite characteristic of the Maldives.

“That, potentially if divers are not experienced, is something that could catch some people out.”

And Dr Fraser also warned that many of the islands are “quite remote” – meaning help could be a long way away in an emergency.

There have been several diving disasters, with experts claiming that some organisations are turning a blind eye to rules and guidance.

This includes safari boats allowing holidaymakers to feed sharks, despite the practice being banned, and diving centres taking tourists down to illegal depths, despite a limit on dives below 30 metres.



Scuba diving consultant Mike Morgan explains that a lack of regulation means higher risks for tourists travelling to the island.

He told The Sun: “Where regulation is not strong or not enforced, there is a reduced sense of care taken by everyone in the chain – whether it’s the boat operator, whether it’s the instructors, whether it’s the tourists or the professionals that are diving.”

While the expert added that holidaymakers can be more prone to accidents as they let their guard down while enjoying their break.



“People are in a holiday mood,” he said. “They may take an extra gas cylinder – but that’s not enough.

“It’s like you and I taking an extra parka and a woollier hat and climbing Everest.”

He also says the Maldives is one of many countries where death figures for diving accidents aren’t accurately recorded.



He claims: If you went around the world and started collecting accurate figures, you would be stunned… there’s a lot that isn’t being recorded by local authorities… It’s quite scary.”

Divers Association of the Maldives co-founder Mohamed Seeneen explained how laws were not being followed by certain diving centres, adding that regulation had been good “until now”.

A safety framework to allow diving under 30 metres in the Maldives needs to be introduced, Seeneen suggested.

“There are a lot of changes that need to take place… new regulations need to come,” he warned.

In 2023, two British men died in separate sea tragedies in the same week.



A 46-year-old died while diving at the popular Hammerhead Shark Point near the atoll of Rasdhoo, and a 65-year-old drowned off the coast of the same island.

And in December last year, Elaine, 70, and her husband Malcolm, 71, tragically died.

The Brit couple were spending Christmas on Ellaidhoo island, where they had spent the festive season for 17 years, when Elaine got into “difficulty” as she tried to resurface from a dive.

Malcolm sounded the alarm after his wife failed to come to the surface – sparking a huge rescue operation.

Elaine was found and rushed to hospital, where she was pronounced dead.



A coroner said Elaine had been “pulled away in a strong current” moments before her death.

Malcolm died five days later on Christmas Eve.

His cause of death was ruled as a result of acute alcohol intoxication, multi-organ dysfunction and cardiac arrest, an inquest heard.

He is understood to have passed away due to the heartbreak of losing his wife, reports say.

The islands have also been plagued by boat accidents and shark attacks.



In November 2024, a 15-year-old British-Singaporean girl was killed after being struck by a boat propeller while on a school trip.

Jenna Chan was on a snorkelling expedition with dozens of fellow students near Dhidhdhoo island – an area notorious for unpredictable and strong currents – when the boat’s engine was suddenly turned on.

A German tourist also died in April this year after a boat propeller hit him near Fenfushi.



There have also been five shark-related incidents this year in the Maldives – including one in April which left the swimmer on life support, according to records seen by The Sun.

Despite being banned, shark feeding is “common with tourists”, Seeneen added.

The holiday hotspot has also seen a string of terrifying boat blazes – with a huge fire engulfing the Yasawa Princess vessel on Christmas Eve last year.

And in November 2024, the Blue Voyager went up in flames while docked in a port.

In May this year, the Emperor Explorer was destroyed by a huge inferno while it was moored near Hulhumalé.



Last month, five Italian tourists died near the Vaavu Atoll. The gruelling recovery operation 60 metres below the surface also took the life of a rescue worker.

According to a mission report, the group were equipped with gear that was “not optimal”.

The harrowing tragedy has so far been ruled as a result of “human error”.

But it has brought the honeymoon hotspot’s safety regulations into the spotlight.

In the Maldives, all recreational diving below 30 metres is forbidden.



Even if a diver has a personal certification to dive deeper than 30 metres, they must still follow the local limit.

Diving below recreational limits is known as technical diving, or tec diving.

Despite the 30 metre rule, certain diving centres “bend the rules” by offering to take tourists below the limit, experts say.

This is because there are no laws created by the Maldivian government to regulate tec diving in the country.

The Sun found one company openly advertising courses for diving and expeditions up to 40 metres, 10 metres below the recreational limit.



Another offers guided tours to explore “breathtaking” underwater dives with “depths reaching up to 70 metres”.

The non-existent regulation for technical diving in the Maldives, despite dives under 30 metres being banned, has therefore created a legal loophole.

It is unclear how many of the 42 diving and snorkelling deaths between 2020 and 2023 in the Maldives were related to technical diving.

Seeneed said local authorities had to wake up to the reality that organisations seemed to be offering to take tourists deeper than local limits.

Seeneen added: “It’s a common practice within the recreational space for some dive centres to bend the rules.”



He called on authorities to introduce laws to stop holidaymakers from being allowed to do technical dives.

Seeneen claimed some organisations also offer expeditions to see thresher sharks, which typically live deeper than 30 metres below the surface, with tourists posting videos of themselves near the sea animals.



However, he does say that the Maldives has some strict safety rules to protect its tourists.

Solo diving is prohibited, and check-dives – to verify each diver’s skills – are mandatory, the expert said.

But a handful of diving centres and smaller islands are still getting away with offering diving tours and expeditions that don’t follow local laws, he said.

“There are certain safari boats which are doing this, certain dive centres in the local islands who might be doing this,” he explained.



“The regulations need to be upgraded, and the tourism ministry needs to do systematic checks on all diving facilities, all snorkelling facilities, all excursion facilities.”

Weighing in on the dangers of holidaying divers pushing past the maximum depth, Morgan said: “Once you start getting beyond the 30 or 40 metre zone… people shouldn’t be [recreationally] diving that deep at all.

“People going deliberately to that depth are putting themselves in a form of jeopardy.”

A combination of unregulated diving, shark incidents, boat accidents and patchy regulation has underscored problematic safety standards in the Maldives as the tourism industry booms.

Just weeks ago, the Foreign Office updated travel advice to the Maldives – warning that some swimming activities “may be fatal”.



The FCDO says: “The sea around the Maldives can have strong tidal currents that can drag you away from the shoreline.”

Warning Brits about the dangers of diving, they added: “Diving safaris are available and may include opportunities to see sharks. Be aware of the potential risks as accidents can occur and, in rare cases, may be fatal.”

Many islands are more than an hour away from the nearest hyperbaric chambers – used to treat decompression sickness – in the case of diving accidents, UK authorities added.

The updated guidance came after the deaths of Elaine and her husband Malcolm.

Following the tragic deaths of the five Italian divers, Maldivian authorities have announced plans to introduce a “Tech-Wreck” law to regulate technical diving.



This will allow tourists in the Maldives – one of a few diving destinations where tec diving is still supposedly banned – to explore beyond 30 metres under proper guidelines.

The Sun has contacted the Maldives Foreign Office and the UK Foreign Office for comment.

News.title: Eating own poo, self-mutilating & driven to kill… The tragic plight of UK zoo animals going crazy by ‘zoochosis’
News.content:
ZOO SHAME Eating own poo, self-mutilating & driven to kill… The tragic plight of UK zoo animals going crazy by ‘zoochosis’

HOLED up in a small basement with no natural light, fresh air, or deep water to dive in, the tragic enclosure of a gentoo penguin in London’s Sea Life aquarium is a far cry from their homeland Antarctica.

But while campaigners, including TV presenter Chris Packham – who called the enclosure a ‘dingy underground bunker’ – fight to improve the birds’ tragic plight, it’s the tip of the iceberg when it comes to troubling conditions at UK zoos and aquariums.





There are currently more than 300 licensed zoos in operation across the country housing tens of thousands of animals, and it’s booming business, with more than 30 million people visiting UK zoos and aquariums every year.

However there are serious concerns that animal suffering is rife in many, due to inadequate enclosures and poor living conditions.

According to Freedom for Animals, tigers and lions for example have around 18,000 times less space in zoos than they would in the wild, while polar bears have one million times less space.

Additionally, there have been endless reports regarding distressed animals injuring themselves or others, as well as displaying alarming and seemingly unnatural behaviours that could be interpreted as signalling severe distress.

Smearing faeces on the walls

Speaking exclusively to The Sun, Peta’s Vice President of Programmes, Elisa Allen, explains: “It can be nearly impossible for a facility to meet the various complex needs of all the various species it holds captive.

“And all too often, the keeping of wild animals in captivity prioritises human entertainment over animals’ well-being.

“Wild animals belong in the wild. Instead of warehousing animals, efforts need to go towards protecting habitats in the wild.

“Confinement and lack of stimulation can result in abnormal and self-destructive behaviour, known as “zoochosis” – animals pacing, swimming or walking in tight circles, rocking, swaying or mutilating themselves.”



Born Free Captivity research and policy manager, Chris Lewis, adds: “There are certain species, as more and more scientific evidence emerges, we realize particularly struggle in captivity.

“Species like elephants and marine mammals – so dolphins and orcas, but also wide-ranging animals like polar bears and big cats and anything that is socially complex as well, like great apes – they’re the ones who struggle.

“Primates, particularly great apes, will engage in eating their own faeces and smearing it on the walls.



“Giraffes in the wild are predominantly grazing the majority of their day but in a zoo they may just get a few branches so for the rest of the day they’ll spend licking on the bars of gates or on the walls of the enclosure.

“You’ll see where the paint is missing from where they’ve been licking it.

“With birds you will see parrots for example plucking out their feathers, and over-preening.”

Visitor concerns

Born Free’s investigations have claimed that many zoos in the UK do not provide their animals with the best possible living conditions or standards of care, and every year, they say they receive many visitor reports concerning animal welfare in UK zoos.

Chris adds: “If you think of what animals are encountering in their wild habitats, zoo enclosures can be quite stale and they don’t change as well so there’s very little variety for them.



“Animals in the wild are also encountering other animals as well.

“Many of the enclosures will just have that single species in there and kept in very small numbers either just themselves or maybe at a pair.

“The other big issue in the UK in particular is the climate.

“Many animals are from a much more tropical climate, so if it’s particularly cold or wet over the winter time a lot of them will spend the majority of their time indoors.



“You may go round looking at a zoo and look at the enclosure and maybe from an aesthetic point of view people may think it looks OK, but then a lot of the animals are spending a lot of their time inside, which is even smaller.

“Another major issue is disease because the animals will be naive to diseases carried by native wildlife, so avian malaria is particularly devastating for penguins and other captive birds. You also have animals from various different parts of the world all living in very close proximity to each other so there is a very high risk of zoonotic disease where these are passed from one animal to another who aren’t used to that.”

No ‘meaningful impact’

Before working for Born Free, Chris previously also trained as a zookeeper specialising in reptile, amphibian and invertebrate care, and worked in educational facilities which kept wild animals to train people to be zoo keepers.

He says: “Ultimately, I, like most people who become zoo keepers, did it because I wanted to help animals, and believed in the conservation of animals.



“But the reality is you get sold, that if you want to save animals, you should go work for a zoo but you get there and you kind of realize that actually what you really doing is you’re just looking after the animals within that zoo which really don’t have much meaningful impact on any conservation at all really.

“They’re just there to bring people through the entrance gates, and then what zoos actually contribute to conservation is actually pretty small because the costs of keeping all these animals is so high.

“The issue when you work in a zoo is you sometimes become almost desensitized to what’s happening because you see it every day, but one of the reasons I stopped doing it was I saw the conditions of certain animals and thought that this isn’t conservation or in the best interests of this animal.



“It’s not only the lions that are just tiny enclosure, walking backwards and forwards, it could be the crocodiles or the turtles which are the tiny pool water, just swimming in circles.

“What you also have to remember as well, particularly with reptiles and amphibians, is what the public sees isn’t necessarily all the animals.

“There are many other animals which are kept ‘off show’ and they will be kept in much less stimulating environments for those animals because they’re not in view of the public.”

Keepers mauled to death

In recent years, questions have arisen about scores of zoos and in some instances, incidents have proven fatal – for both humans and the animals.

In 2013 South Lakes Wild Animal Park (later known as Safari Zoo Cumbria) keeper Sarah McClay, 23, was mauled to death by a Sumatran tiger that got through an unlocked gate.



Then there was the tragic death of Rosa King, 33, who was attacked by a tiger called Cicip while cleaning windows at Hamerton Zoo Park back in 2017. She suffered “traumatic” injuries, including a severed spinal cord.

In 2014, a male keeper was found seriously injured in water in the rhino enclosure at Whipsnade Zoo with injuries to the chest, abdomen and pelvis, while in 2024 a zookeeper lost the tip of his finger while feeding a Siberian tiger at Big Cat Sanctuary, Kent.

Chris adds: “We mustn’t forget that a number of animals kept in a zoo are inherently dangerous.

“They retain their wild behaviours and instincts even when they’re born in captivity.

“There’s numerous instances of people and other zoo animals being killed, big cats, rhinos, because they retain wild instincts.”



Electrocuted and partially eaten

In 2024 Safari Zoo Cumbria, once dubbed Britain’s worst, finally shut down, after almost 500 animals died in the three years between 2013 and 2016, including a tortoise electrocuted on fencing, a squirrel found dead behind a radiator and two snow leopards who were found partially eaten.

Then there’s an ongoing issue with the use of euthanasia.

Just last month Kent animal conservation charity Wildwood Trust said it had “no choice” but to euthanise its entire wolf pack.

They said the “heartbreaking decision” was needed to “prevent further suffering” after three of the five wolves sustained serious injuries from infighting.

Chris says: “This is the issue of keeping socially complex animals in a confined environment. “With wolves there will be an alpha male and an alpha female, but there will always be, as those animals get older, there will be challenges to that authority, and often when those things occur in the wild and that individual is overthrown – if they aren’t killed by the usurper they will disperse and either form their own pack or continue to live by themselves. In captivity, that option isn’t available.



“You see that with wolves but it can also happen with meerkats, and all socially group-living animals, where there’s a hierarchy and the hierarchy is disrupted.

“Great apes are another prime example where this occurs.

“Zoos are actually struggling with an over-abundance of males and where to put them. That’s why there was a story a few years ago that they were considering culling male gorillas because they had too many.

“I don’t know how many times it has to keep happening before there’s something done. We shouldn’t be keeping these socially complex species in a captive environment where they can’t cope with the social dynamics when it goes wrong.”

Morally conflicted

Zoos often claim they contribute to species conservation and public education, to justify the keeping and breeding of wild animals in captivity.



As a community, the British and Irish Association of Zoos and Aquariums say the picture painted by activists resembles 50 years in the past, rather than the modern reality, and they make a significant contribution to conservation, with members supporting more than 1,000 conservation projects.

Many of their member zoos and aquariums have charitable status and are all involved in conservation projects either directly or by partnering with conservation charities and non-governmental organizations.

They argue recent conservation achievements include the reintroduction of critically endangered bongo antelope to the wild, the first genomic sequencing of the endangered barbary macaque, and the wide-spread rewilding of beavers, water voles and even rare moths in Britain.

But Peta’s Elisa Allen, says: “Most animals confined in zoos and aquariums are not threatened or endangered.

“There are now more tigers in zoos than in the wild. If we really want to help these endangered animals, we must target the root cause of species extinction, which is habitat destruction and hunting, because all the cages in the world are never going to stop animals from becoming extinct.”



So if they’re not releasing many animals to the wild, are they donating money? The British and Irish Association of Zoos and Aquariums say in the past six years their members have spent over £187 million on conservation; money that would not exist without zoos and aquariums.

However, Chris says: “In reality reports Born Free have done in the past shows that they’re donating maybe four percent – if that – of the income to supporting conservation in the wild.”

If we want to support the world’s wildlife, Chris argues visiting a zoo is not the way forward. Finally, he adds: “We find it a lot that adults are morally conflicted as to whether to go to a zoo, but they feel like they should take their children because then the children can learn about animals – but the reality is the educational benefits of zoos are highly questionable.

“There is no hard line evidence that there is an educational benefit from visiting a zoo.

“We would argue children can learn just as much by getting out and about in nature, in parks, in green spaces. Children are obsessed with space and dinosaurs, but they’ve never seen either of those in person.



“What we’d recommend is that if you want to support the conservation of wild animals, donate your money directly to the organisations that are doing that work on the ground because you will be told by going to a zoo, you’re helping to support conservation but actually, in reality – the vast majority of your money is basically paying to keep the lights on at the zoo.”

A spokesperson for BIAZA adds: “As a charity, BIAZA are proud that good zoos and aquariums are guardians of nature and fighting back against extinction. The public and respected scientists alike know that good zoos and aquariums have care for nature at their very heart, that’s why they are the top choice of a day out, among the most visited attractions in the country, and enjoy huge public support for their conservation, education and research roles.

“The picture painted by activists resembles 50 years in the past, rather than the modern reality. BIAZA members are rightly proud of how they look after their animals.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Dedicated, expert keepers provide round the clock care for some of the world’s most incredible animals. They ensure that their mental and physical needs are a priority and the picture Born Free presents of abnormal and self-destructive behaviours being common is thankfully a thing of the past.

“As a charity dedicated to world-class animal care, BIAZA’s accreditation programme ensures animals at our members are looked after to the very highest standards. We are proud that our member zoos and aquariums are brilliant homes for their animals.”

News.title: Red Arrows flight path today: Route map and transit times for Torbay and Midlands Air Festival displays
News.content:
THE Red Arrows are taking on one of the busiest days of their 2026 calendar today, performing spectacular stunts over three counties.

With the RAF aerobatic team set to take off with seven planes instead of nine, here’s everything you need to know about the flight path.





What is the Red Arrows route today?

You can see today’s full flight path below, per the website Military Airshows:

The Red Arrows are scheduled to depart Exeter Airport at 11.45am on Saturday morning, and will perform a display above Torbay at midday.

They will then set out from Exeter again at 2.41pm this afternoon, and make an afternoon flypast over Upper Wardington at around 2.54pm.

After time on the ground at East Midlands Airport, the Reds will take off again at 5.48pm for the evening’s Midlands Air Festival display at Ragley Hall, before returning to the airport for 6.33pm.

The full route today is as follows:

11.45am: Exeter Airport

11.59am: vicinity of Totnes

12.00pm: Torbay Display

12.24pm: north of Sidmouth

12.28pm: Exeter Airport

2.41pm: Exeter Airport

2.54pm: Upper Wardington Flypast, Oxfordshire

2.55pm: east of Farthingstone, Northamptonshire

3.00pm: vicinity of Ratby, Leicestershire

3.02pm: south of East Leake, Nottinghamshire

3.03pm: East Midlands Airport

5.48pm: East Midlands Airport

5.50pm: north-east of Whitwick, Leicestershire

5.53pm: north of Rugby, Warwickshire

5.56pm: north of Lighthorne, Warwickshire

5.58pm: north-west of Redditch, Worcestershire

5.59pm: vicinity of Redditch, Worcestershire

6pm: Midlands Air Festival display, Ragley Hall, Warwickshire

6.21pm: east of Evesham, Worcestershire

6.22pm: west of Tredington, Warwickshire

6.24pm: north-east of Kineton, Warwickshire

6.27pm: north-east of Clifton upon Dunsmore, Warwickshire

6.32pm: north of Breaston, Derbyshire

6.33pm: East Midlands Airport

Route and times may change due to weather or other operational requirements.

Why are there only seven Red Arrows in 2026?

In a shake-up announced on Saturday, May 23, the Red Arrows are now performing with seven aircraft – Reds 1 to 7 – instead of their traditional nine for the bulk of their 2026 displays.



The change has been brought in to help manage the team’s ageing Hawk T1 jets as they prepare to transition to a future aircraft type.

An RAF spokesperson said: “The Red Arrows are the pride of the nation, known globally for their world-class precision, speed, and teamwork.

“The Red Arrows will fly in a nine-aircraft formation for HM The King’s Birthday Flypast and the 4th of July 250 Commemorations in the USA this year.

“For other displays, they will operate with seven aircraft, continuing to deliver high-quality, engaging displays at air shows and events across the UK, mainland Europe and further afield.”

What time is the Upper Wardington flypast?

The Red Arrows are scheduled to perform their flypast over Upper Wardington in Oxfordshire at 2.54pm this afternoon.



The team will arrive in the area from the south-west, having passed over Devon, Somerset, Wiltshire and Gloucestershire, with the flypast forming part of their transit from Exeter Airport up to East Midlands Airport.

The Reds will track south-east of Shutford in Oxfordshire at 2.53pm before reaching Upper Wardington itself a minute later, then continuing on east of Farthingstone in Northamptonshire at 2.55pm.

What time is the Red Arrows Midlands Air Festival display?

The Red Arrows will take to the skies above Ragley Hall at 6pm this evening for the Midlands Air Festival display, with the team’s broader route window running from 5.48pm to 6.33pm.

They are set to take off from East Midlands Airport at 5.48pm and track south-west via north-east of Whitwick at 5.50pm.

The team will then pass north of Rugby at 5.53pm, before continuing north of Lighthorne at 5.56pm.



They will track north-west of Redditch at 5.58pm, before passing through the vicinity of Redditch at 5.59pm.

The Reds will then arrive over Ragley Hall in Warwickshire for the display at 6pm.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Following the showpiece, the team will return north-east via Evesham, Tredington, Kineton, Clifton upon Dunsmore and Breaston.

They will then land back at East Midlands Airport at 6.33pm.

News.title: Trump continues to weigh up peace deal after 2-hour crunch talks as five US servicemen injured by Iranian missile debris
News.content:
RAGING ON Trump continues to weigh up peace deal after 2-hour crunch talks as five US servicemen injured by Iranian missile debris

FIVE US service members have been injured by an Iranian missile strike in Kuwait as the US-Tehran ceasefire agreement hangs by a thread.

Kuwaiti air defenses intercepted the Fateh-110 missile, but falling debris struck the Ali Al Salem air base.





Around five people, including active duty personnel, suffered minor injuries, according to Bloomberg.

The strike also damaged two $30million US MQ-9 Reaper strike drones.

It comes as US President Donald Trump weighs up a peace deal with Iran to extend a fragile ceasefire.

America warned on Saturday it is “more than capable” of resuming the war in the Middle East as Trump said any deal must stick to his red lines.



This includes Tehran never being able to develop nuclear weapons – a major sticking point in negotiations so far.

The White House had signalled Trump was close to a decision on an initial deal after weeks of mixed signals.

But US sources told AFP a two-hour meeting in the White House Situation Room on Friday ground to a halt without a deal.

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said on Saturday the US still has “plentiful munitions” to keep blitzing Iran if necessary.



There are 50,000 US troops still stationed across the region and prepared to resume hostilities, he added.

Efforts to strike a deal were thrown into doubt earlier this week when the US struck a port in southern Iran which was met with retaliatory fire.

The Ali Al Salem Air Base came under fire from another Iranian missile earlier this week – which was reportedly intercepted.



It came after Trump’s forces shot down four Iranian attack drones and blitzed a military site in Bandar Abbas that US officials said were preparing to launch a fifth UAV.

Trump’s key peace deal priorities include Iran agreeing to never develop nuclear weapons and the re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz.

But Iran has pushed back on the conditions, refusing to bow to Trump’s demands.

Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told state media the Islamic republic “said goodbye to the language of ‘must’ 47 years ago”.

Negotiations continue, he said, but “no final agreement has been reached yet.”



In a Truth Social post on Friday, Trump said Tehran would remove mines from the Strait and end its closure of the key waterway with “no tolls,” while the US would lift its parallel blockade of Iranian ports.

The two countries would also coordinate on removing and destroying Iran’s enriched uranium.

Meanwhile Tehran has demanded “the immediate release of $12billion in frozen Iranian assets” before moving forward with talks, Iran’s Fars news agency said.

During a Wednesday cabinet meeting Trump had hinted he was optimistic that a deal would be reached soon.

But he added: “Maybe we have to go back and finish it.”

News.title: Shocked mums hit out after spotting gruesome passage about Jack the Ripper in popular kids’ book
News.content:
MUMS told of their shock after spotting a gruesome passage about Jack the Ripper in a popular kids’ book.

A page in ‘Whoosh Around the Mulberry Bush’ features part of a report in which gobsmacked parents can make out the words ‘throat cut’ and ‘prostitution’.





One blasted: “Some of the sleuths in the comments have worked out it’s not an autopsy but taken from a passage about Jack the Ripper or the Boston Strangler, which makes sense.”

Kimberley Mills, observing the collage depiction of a flower, said: “That’s so creepy.”

Mum Jodi joked: “Someone might wanna check that author’s hard drive lol.”

The colourful page shows insects crawling around a garden with the words, ‘Here we go round the flower bed on a sweet smelling morning’.

One of the leaves on the flowers is made up of an article appearing to depict the crimes of Jack the Ripper – an unidentified serial killer active around impoverished Whitechapel in London, in 1888, who is said to have killed five victims.

Model mum Katie Green piled in online after discovering the inappropriate text in her child’s book.

She said: “Hi OxUniPress, why does my infant son’s book contain a sinister passage about Jack the Ripper?”

Jan Omerod’s 2007 hit ‘Whoosh Around the Mulberry Bush’, illustrated by Lindsey Gardiner, starts with children dancing before showing animal capers, including hens pecking around a chicken coop, monkeys swinging around jungle vines, polar bears and arctic hares sliding around icicles and zebras kicking their heels around a waterhole.



The text can be sung to the rhythm of the kids’ song, ‘Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush’.

Oxford University Press told The Sun they take the “integrity of our children’s publishing very seriously and appreciate having this brought to our attention”.

A spokesperson said illustrations in the book, which is no longer in print, “use a range of collage techniques and any perceived links to specific texts or references are unintentional.”

News.title: NHS help for kids on vapes amid staggering £6bn black market
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: NHS help for kids on vapes amid staggering £6bn black market

Prof Rachel Isba of Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool is supporting NHS services across the country to help youngsters kick the habit

View 3 Images Help for teen vapers will be incorporated into NHS services across the country (Image: Getty Images)

Support for youngsters hooked on vapes is set to be incorporated into NHS services across the country.

‌



Last year Liverpool’s Alder Hey Children’s Hospital opened the UK’s first and only pilot clinic for 11 to 15-year-olds addicted to e-cigs. And now the programme’s lead medic Prof Rachel Isba is working with other trusts to help more teens kick the habit.

‌



She told us: “I am currently supporting colleagues across the UK to incorporate elements of the pilot clinic into their everyday practice and services to support children and young people following the completion of the pilot. These services might be within clinical services, drug and alcohol services or existing stop smoking services. Everyone is seeing this as an important issue.”

‌



View 3 Images Alder Hey Children’s Hospital opened the UK’s first and only pilot clinic for 11 to 15-year-olds addicted to e-cigs (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Dodgy high street bosses using vape shops or barbers as fronts face fresh crackdown READ MORE :

Help offered could include nicotine replacement therapy, counselling and education around health and wellbeing. Prof Isba, a consultant in paediatric public health medicine, also hopes to help paediatricians have conversations about vaping as part of regular check-ups, and to involve other local services like safeguarding where appropriate.

‌



The move comes as Monday marks a year since the government ban on disposable vapes came into force. The measure was introduced to protect children’s health and curb the growing environmental damage caused by millions of improperly discarded plastic devices and lithium-ion batteries.

But 12 months on, there is not yet clear evidence on whether the ban is having an impact on their use among young people. More than six million vapes and vape pods are still being discarded every week in the UK, according to research by recycling campaign group Material Focus. And there is a thriving black market worth an estimated £6 billion annually.

View 3 Images Help offered could include nicotine replacement therapy, counselling and education around health and wellbeing (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

Around five to nine per cent of 11 to 15-year-olds currently vape, according to NHS surveys and Action on Smoking and Health data. And between 5.4 and 5.6 million adults puff too, making up about 10 per cent of over-18s.

For the first time, vapers now outnumber traditional cigarette smokers, who make up roughly 9.1 per cent of the population. Alder Hey’s vaping clinic was a pilot funded by NHS Cheshire and Merseyside to explore approaches to vaping cessation support for children and young people. The pilot has now ended and the hospital is exploring future funding options.

News.title: HMRC issues pension tax update ahead of rate increase
News.content:
HMRC issues pension tax update ahead of rate increase

The tax rules and allowances differ depending on your situation

View 2 Images HMRC has clarified the tax rules that apply to pensioners (Image: Getty)

HMRC has released an update to clarify how tax rules apply to pensioners. Now is a good time to check the rules as the rates you have to pay are set to rise shortly.

‌



A person contacted the tax authority via social media seeking clarification on how the rules operate. They asked: "Can you confirm that a pensioner does not have to pay tax on the first £1,000 of interest earned on savings." In accordance with the personal savings allowance, those on the basic rate of income tax can earn up to £1,000 in savings interest each tax year completely tax-free. However, the allowance is halved for higher rate taxpayers, dropping to £500, while those on the additional rate receive no allowance whatsoever and must pay tax on all interest earnings.

‌



This differs from savings accumulated in cash ISAs, where all interest earnings are entirely exempt from tax. Similarly, stocks and shares held within an ISA wrapper are free from tax on any investment growth.

‌



Tax rules explained

Responding to the query, HMRC spelled out the rules. It said: "Pensioners have the same rules as everyone else. So if they are a basic rate taxpayer only, then yes they have a £1,000 tax-free allowance."

State Pensioners to face major tax change

The rate applied to any taxable interest mirrors your income tax rate, meaning basic rate taxpayers pay 20 per cent, higher rate taxpayers pay 40 per cent, and those on the additional rate pay 45 per cent.

‌



However, it is worth bearing in mind that the rules are set to change in the near future. From April 2027, the rate paid on interest earnings will rise by two percentage points, meaning those on the basic rate will see it climb to 22 per cent.

Higher rate taxpayers will face an increase to 42 per cent, while those on the additional rate will be required to pay 47 per cent. Further changes arriving in April 2027 could also push up the tax you pay on your savings.

View 2 Images HMRC has clarified the tax rules that apply to pensioners (Image: Getty)

Article continues below

Tax allowance changes coming up

The ISA allowance is effectively being reduced. At present, you can deposit £20,000 into ISAs and divide this however you wish between cash ISAs and stocks and shares ISAs.

Under the new regulations, however, you will only be able to allocate up to £12,000 of the allowance as you see fit. The remaining £8,000 must be placed into stocks and shares ISAs.

That said, many older savers will be exempt from these new rules. Those aged 65 and over will keep the existing £20,000 allowance.

Kitchen cupboard item will keep your whites 'crisp and clean' for longer

News.title: Resident says 'collapsing wall' is neighbour's - but people spot key detail in picture
News.content:
Resident says 'collapsing wall' is neighbour's - but people spot key detail in picture

Resident has been accused of trespassing by neighbour but claims land registry is in their favour - however a picture might suggest otherwise

View Image The wall in question might be the responsibility of the neighbour, according to plans, but there is a key issue in the picture, experts said (Image: Reddit)

A homeowner just bought a new house - and has been locked in a dispute with a neighbour over a wall which appears to be collapsing. The issue emerged as they pleaded for help to see if they can definitively assign responsibility.

‌



They said the Land Registry title plan had the key ‘T’ designation suggesting their neighbour was responsible for the brick wall. They said on Reddit: “I bought my house last year, and there is a brick retaining wall along one side of the garden. The wall supports the neighbour’s higher garden level.

‌



“According to the Land Registry title plan, there are inward “T” marks on the boundary opposite from this wall, indicating that the neighbour is responsible for maintaining the retaining wall.”

‌



The resident said that when they bought the property the wall was ‘already in a poor condition’ but that in the last 12 months it has ‘deteriorated significantly’. They said: “I tried to speak to the neighbour in person several times but wasn’t able to have a conversation, so I sought free legal advice at a local community centre. The solicitor there confirmed (based on the title plan) that the wall appears to be the neighbour’s responsibility.

“Following the above advice, I sent the neighbour a letter explaining that the wall appears to be their responsibility and that its condition poses a potential risk to our property. I also asked if they intended to repair it as a result, and noted that we would hold them responsible for any damage if the wall were to collapse. They did not respond.”

A contractor has told the resident that it would cost £6,500 to repair the wall ‘He also said it could collapse at any time.’ They then added: “After the contractor visited, the neighbour approached me and accused us of trespassing (the contractor briefly stepped onto their driveway to assess the situation), stated they will not take responsibility for the wall, said that if we want to fix it, it must be at our expense, claimed we would need their permission and to give 28 days’ notice before doing any work, as the wall sits on the boundary line.

‌



“From what I can see, the wall is on/very close to the boundary line, but it supports their land, not ours.” They asked if they might be able to recover the costs if they have it repaired, and how legally binding the title deeds are.

Some people noticed a key detail in the picture. One said: “That wire thing looks suspiciously like the original boundary line, with the wall on your side of the boundary.” Another added: “Definitely original boundary posts indicate wall is your responsibility. Those things have been up since the 1930’s.”

One said: “This is the most important observation here - there is an old fence (possibly 80-100 years old) between your neighbours fence and the wall. While we can all look at deeds and argue until the cows come home whether that old fence is yours or theirs, the wall is clearly on your side of that fence and hence (definitely) on your land and (presumably) yours. Fix it or wait for it to fail.”

‌



However there was hope with one person suggesting that the neighbour had simply tried to ignore the problem: “If the T on the deeds point into your neighbours property, then they are responsible as the wall needs repair/rebuilding

“It would appear that your neighbour has chosen to ignore the issue & built another fence. Whatever you do, do NOT touch the wall. It could be structural & removing it, could lead to serious issues, if the neighbours garden is that much higher.

“It will cost money to seek a specialist Solicitor but will potentially save lots of money & legal disputes in the future, so regard it as an investment”

Article continues below

And the homeowner finally said: “Many thanks for your advice. I tried contacting the council last year but they stated that it’s a civil matter and they didn’t want to get involved. I will try again and stress that this is now an emergency. I will give the home insurance another call too.”

News.title: Norovirus symptom you may notice in your legs
News.content:
Norovirus symptom you may notice in your legs

UKHSA reminds people that norovirus doesn't just spread in the winter

View Image Noroviruses spreads all year round (Image: SimpleImages via Getty Images)

People are being warned that an illness commonly referred to as a "winter bug" actually circulates throughout the entire year. And there are some less well-known warning signs to watch for.

‌



Anyone who develops norovirus should remain away from work or school, as well as care homes and hospitals, for 48 hours after symptoms disappear, in an effort to prevent transmission. UKHSA previously posted on X, formerly Twitter: "Vomiting or diarrhoea in spring? It could still be #Norovirus. Despite being known as the 'winter vomiting bug', norovirus can spread all year round."

‌



UKHSA guidance further adds that norovirus "is able to spread easily through communities and so outbreaks are common in settings where individuals have close contact such as hospitals, care homes, schools and nurseries." Symptoms usually start between 12 and 48 hours after catching the virus, with people being most infectious while symptomatic.

‌



However, it is possible to "shed" the virus, contaminating surfaces, objects or even food, both before and after displaying symptoms. It's therefore crucial to regularly and thoroughly wash your hands with warm water and soap, and to avoid preparing food for others.

The UKHSA also warns that alcohol-based hand sanitisers are not effective against norovirus. Typical symptoms include nausea, diarrhoea, and/or vomiting.

Article continues below

However, some norovirus sufferers may also experience headaches, fever, and aching in their legs and/or arms. Any clothing or bedding that could be contaminated should be washed at 60C.

Rescue teams in Laos are racing against time to free four men still trapped in a flooded cave, 10 days after they became stranded, while searching for two others who remain missing.

The urgent operation follows the successful evacuation of the first survivor on Friday, offering a glimmer of hope in the perilous mission.

Rescuers are optimistic about extracting the remaining four men later on Saturday, having previously deemed them not ready for removal.

Efforts are focused on draining more water from the cave system as the search for the two missing individuals continues. Norrased Palasing, a Thai cave diver involved in the operation, affirmed the commitment on his Facebook page: "One person has made it out safely, and we will not stop until the remaining four make it home too."

The initial evacuation on Friday took about 30 minutes. Videos captured the moment the first survivor emerged from the water alongside a diver, gasping for breath before struggling through a narrow, flooded passage.

He rose unsteadily to his feet, his hands visibly injured, as rescuers cautioned each other. He was then wrapped in a foil blanket and helped into a seated position. Another video showed him exiting the cave’s entrance, a lamp strapped to his forehead, walking unsteadily with assistance before being handed over to other team members amidst a waiting crowd.

The villagers had reportedly entered the cave last week in search of valuable minerals when flash flooding blocked their exit. One villager managed to escape and alert authorities to the seven left behind. Five were found alive on Wednesday and identified by their first names: Khamla, Mued, Ee, Ing, and Laen. It remains unclear which of them was evacuated on Friday. The trapped men had been supplied with water, soft food, and foil blankets, though videos from inside the cave suggested their conditions were deteriorating.

Rescuers evacuate the first of the trapped villagers from a flooded cave in Xaisomboun, Laos, on 29 May 2026 ( AP )

The international rescue effort involves teams from Laos, Thailand, Japan, and Malaysia, with Indonesian, French, and Australian specialists also arriving at the rugged site in the central province of Xaisomboun, about 120km north of the capital Vientiane. Many of the divers have prior experience from the complex 2018 cave rescue of 12 schoolboys and their football coach in northern Thailand.

The challenges facing the rescuers are immense. Thai rescuer Kengkaj Bongkawong of the Metta Tham Rescue Kalasin detailed the treacherous conditions in a video shot on Friday, just an hour before the first evacuation. A station has been established in a large chamber, accessible only after navigating over 200 metres of twisting, narrow, flooded passages with jagged walls. From there, divers must navigate a 30-metre flooded tunnel to reach the trapped men.

"To dive in a cave, there are issues with the temperature, narrow areas, control of movement, and managing the panic of the survivor, which will be difficult, but we have to do it," Kengkaj said.

Guiding survivors with no diving experience through zero-visibility water presents a significant risk. A video showed Thai diver Norrased and Finnish diver Mikko Paasi instructing the men on using diving gear and breathing techniques.

"All the way, breathe through your mouth only. Do not ever breathe with your nose, do you understand?" Norrased emphasised during the session.

Rescuers are also preparing to extend their search for the two missing villagers. Kengkaj indicated plans to explore an area 20 to 25 metres deeper inside the cave, beyond where the survivors were located. However, he cautioned that this section is heavily flooded. "That area has a lot of water. The water goes there because it’s even deeper than this place," he explained.
